name: Ziltivekimab
summary: Ziltivekimab (NN6018) is Novo Nordisk's wholly owned, once-monthly subcutaneous anti-IL-6 antibody, bought with Corvidia in 2020. ZEUS (ASCVD with CKD and inflammation) missed its MACE endpoint on 31 July 2026 (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.88-1.11), and Novo stopped HERMES and ATHENA in heart failure for futility on 4-7 September 2026. ARTEMIS (NCT06118281) continues as planned. It is a 10,000-patient, event-driven 3-point MACE trial started within 36-48 hours of an acute MI, with primary completion 2027-01-29 and a readout in H1 2027. It is a Phase 3 outcomes trial that can support a filing by itself, so the asset keeps a standalone path in Myocardial Infarction and is not refused. Heart Failure is not modelled. Price anchor: Repatha, the injectable antibody used for secondary prevention after MI, at $4,266 per Medicare Part D beneficiary in 2024. Uptake anchor: US PCSK9 antibody starts within a year of an MI (0.4% Medicare, 0.7% commercial, 2015-2020), scaled to 2024 by the class's Part D beneficiary growth, about 1.7% of each year's eligible heart attacks.

therapy_mode.source: ARTEMIS design, NCT06118281 (HRA research summary 4979, https://www.hra.nhs.uk/planning-and-improving-research/application-summaries/research-summaries/4979-artemis-ziltivekimab-vs-placebo-on-cvot-in-patients-with-acute-mi/; UC San Diego trial listing, https://clinicaltrials.ucsd.edu/trial/NCT06118281): a subcutaneous loading dose as early as possible after the invasive procedure and within 36 hours (STEMI) or 48 hours (NSTEMI) of admission, then once monthly, added to standard of care, over a treatment period estimated at up to 2 years. The trial is event-driven
therapy_mode.note: Monthly maintenance dosing, so chronic. Case against: the trial's own treatment period is about 2 years and the label may follow it. The discontinuation below gives a mean time on drug of about 2 years (1/0.505), close to that period, so a fixed course and a chronic line land in about the same place
therapy_mode.check: Status first: ARTEMIS is still running. The book's ClinicalTrials.gov row for NCT06118281, fetched 2026-09-24, reads Active not recruiting, primary completion 2027-01-29 (estimated), last update 2026-09-09. The changes table logged that update on 2026-09-10: primary completion slipped from 2026-12-14 and status moved from Recruiting to Active not recruiting (enrolment closed; nothing stopped). Novo's ZEUS release of 31 July 2026 (GlobeNewswire; 6-K f6k_073126) and the September coverage of the HERMES and ATHENA stops (STAT 2026-09-07, Clinical Trials Arena, Endpoints, from search excerpts) all say ARTEMIS continues as planned, readout H1 2027. Design, from search excerpts of the HRA summary 4979 and the UCSD and CT.gov listings: loading dose subcutaneously as early as possible after the invasive procedure, at the latest within 36 h of admission for STEMI or 48 h for NSTEMI. Then once monthly, added to standard of care, over a treatment period 'estimated up to 2 years'. So monthly maintenance makes it chronic. The 2-year period is correctly the case against it, and 1/0.505 = 1.98 years mean time on drug squares with it. Amass TrialCore was unavailable (subscription limit), so the registry facts rest on the book's own fetch of the same day

list_price_per_patient.source: lookup.py demand Repatha: 'Repatha (3 presentations)', CMS Medicare Part D 2024, $1,962,120,377 over 459,932 beneficiaries = $4,266 per beneficiary
list_price_per_patient.note: Judgement on the comparator. Repatha is the closest marketed comparator in the same setting: a self-injected antibody, dosed every two weeks or monthly, used for secondary prevention after MI, and the largest by Medicare use. Case against: Praluent Pen, whose ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial enrolled patients after an acute coronary syndrome, reads lower at $3,683 (Part D 2024). Leqvio reads $6,135 on Part B. IL-6 antibodies priced for rheumatology read far higher: Kevzara $27,534 (Part D 2024) and Actemra $26,606 (Part D 2024). Novo would price for a mass cardiovascular population, not a rheumatology one. Per-beneficiary spend covers part-years, so it sits under an annual list price. Discrepancy to flag: the enlicitide seed quotes 'Repatha SureClick' at $4,470 ($1,709,589,708 over 382,461). The current drug_demand table has no such row, only 'Repatha (3 presentations)', which is used here
list_price_per_patient.check: lookup.py demand Repatha: only 'Repatha (3 presentations)', Part D only, 2024 $1,962,120,377 / 459,932 = $4,266.1 per beneficiary, so 0.004266 mm USD per patient-year is right. The comparators in the note also check: Praluent Pen 2024 $3,683, Leqvio Part B 2024 $6,135, Kevzara Part D 2024 $27,534, Actemra (2 presentations) Part D 2024 $26,606. The enlicitide seed's 'Repatha SureClick' $4,470 (382,461 beneficiaries) has no row in drug_demand; the discrepancy is real. I tested whether an anti-inflammatory post-MI drug prices differently. (a) The only FDA-approved anti-inflammatory for cardiovascular risk reduction is Lodoco (colchicine 0.5 mg, June 2023). Drugs.com puts its cash price at about $531 for 30 tablets, about $6,460 a year. That is a retail cash price, not WAC, and the book has no CMS row for it. It lists above Repatha, but its use is thin because generic colchicine sells for cents. (b) IL-6 antibodies priced for rheumatology run about $27,000 (above). (c) Ilaris, the IL-1b antibody behind CANTOS that was never approved for cardiovascular use, runs $147,058 per Part D beneficiary in 2024, a rare-disease price. (d) Searches found no published or guided ziltivekimab price: analyst coverage gives peak sales only (Guggenheim about $3bn, Citi about $1.7bn risk-adjusted). So the anti-inflammatory case points higher, not lower: the mass-cardiovascular band runs from $3,683 (Praluent) to about $6,100-6,460 (Leqvio; Lodoco cash), and $4,266 sits at its low end. Repatha remains the closest comparator for the setting and route under the house convention, a conservative choice. The judgement label and the case against both hold

gross_to_net_pct.source: house convention on a CMS Part D per-beneficiary price (backend/gross_to_net.py: halving lands at a median 96% of CMS's own negotiated net prices). The same value the enlicitide, AZD0780, olpasiran and lepodisiran seeds take
gross_to_net_pct.note: Direction checked: 0.5 off list, so net is $2,133 per patient-year. Repatha is a Part D drug (lookup.py demand shows only Part D rows), so the Part B deduction does not apply
gross_to_net_pct.check: Repatha's demand rows are Part D only (lookup.py demand), so the Part D convention applies: PART_D_CONVENTION = 0.5 in backend/gross_to_net.py, whose docstring gives the median 96% of CMS negotiated prices. Direction right: 0.5 is the share off list, so net = $4,266 x 0.5 = $2,133. The Part B deduction (0.056604) would be wrong here. Same value as the enlicitide, AZD0780, olpasiran and lepodisiran seeds (lookup.py seed)

discontinuation_pct.unit: share of treated stock stopping per year
discontinuation_pct.source: PCSK9 antibody discontinuation by 12 months: 55.8% in Medicare and 41.5% in commercial US claims (Navar AM et al., Am J Cardiol 2025;242:1-9, doi:10.1016/j.amjcard.2024.12.029), as carried by the book's AZD0780 seed. Weighted by payer mix of US NSTEMI admissions: Medicare 62.9%, all other payers 37.1% (Vallabhajosyula S et al., Ann Transl Med 2021;9(13):1075, doi:10.21037/atm-20-5193, National Inpatient Sample 2000-2017). 0.629 x 0.558 + 0.371 x 0.415 = 0.505
discontinuation_pct.note: Judgement: the same class of drug (a self-injected antibody for secondary prevention) and the same payer weights as penetration_peak_pct. Non-Medicare payers (Medicaid, uninsured, other: 13.0 points of the 37.1) take the commercial rate. Case for higher: a post-MI anti-inflammatory with no lipid number to track may be dropped sooner once the acute phase passes. Case for lower: a monthly dose is less burdensome than Repatha's fortnightly option
discontinuation_pct.check: Navar AM et al., Am J Cardiol 2025;242:1-9 (PMID 39826880, doi 10.1016/j.amjcard.2024.12.029), abstract: PCSK9i mAb discontinuation by 12 months 41.5% commercial and 55.8% Medicare. The AZD0780 seed carries the same figures. Vallabhajosyula S et al., Ann Transl Med 2021;9(13):1075 (PMID 34422987, doi 10.21037/atm-20-5193), NIS 2000-2017, 7,290,565 NSTEMI admissions: Medicare 62.9%, Medicaid 6.1%, private 24.1%, uninsured 4.6%, other 2.3%, so non-Medicare 37.1% of which 13.0 points are not private. Recomputed: 0.629 x 0.558 + 0.371 x 0.415 = 0.350982 + 0.153965 = 0.504947, so 0.505. A labelled judgement (class analogue, payer weights) with cases both ways

forecast_start_year.source: NCT06118281 primary completion 2027-01-29 (estimated; context file and book trials table, last update 2026-09-09). Novo expects the ARTEMIS readout in H1 2027 (https://www.statnews.com/2026/09/07/novo-nordisk-heart-studies-inflammation-ziltivekimab/; https://www.clinicaltrialsarena.com/news/novo-nordisk-ziltivekimab-phase-iii-terminations/)
forecast_start_year.note: Judgement on the timeline. A readout in H1 2027, a BLA in the second half of 2027 and a standard review put approval around late 2028, so 2029 is the first full year. That is the same PCD-to-revenue lag the tulisokibart and duvakitug seeds use: about two calendar years. Case against: a priority review would not move the first full year, but any filing slip or an FDA request for more safety data after ZEUS makes it 2030
forecast_start_year.check: Primary completion 2027-01-29 (estimated) in the book's CT.gov row fetched 2026-09-24, slipped from 2026-12-14 on the 2026-09-09 update. Readout H1 2027 is in Novo's 31 July ZEUS release and the 7 September STAT and Clinical Trials Arena coverage (search excerpts). H1 2027 readout, BLA in H2 2027, and a standard 12-month BLA review puts approval in late 2028, so 2029 is the first full year, later than the 2027 default, as the brief allows. The lag matches the seeds cited: tulisokibart primary completion 2026-08-01 gives forecast 2028; duvakitug primary completion 2028-09-21 gives forecast 2030 (lookup.py seed and book trials). Two calendar years in each. A labelled judgement with a case against

exus_multiple.source: Repatha FY2025: $1,353mm outside the US against $1,663mm US (Amgen 10-K 0000318154-26-000010; book asset_revenue_regions, sec_fsds). 1,353 / 1,663 = 0.8136
exus_multiple.note: Judgement: the price comparator's own filed split. Novo has no marketed cardiovascular antibody to read a split from. Case for higher: Leqvio reads 623/575 = 1.08 (Novartis 20-F 0001114448-26-000004), and ARTEMIS runs in 24 countries. Case against: ex-US payers restricted PCSK9 antibodies harder than US ones for years, and the engine applies this multiple to patients at the US net price
exus_multiple.check: book asset_revenue_regions, Repatha FY2025 (sec_fsds, 10-K 0000318154-26-000010): US $1,663,000,000 and NonUs $1,353,000,000. 1,353 / 1,663 = 0.81359, so 0.8136. Leqvio FY2025 (20-F 0001114448-26-000004): US 575, rest of world 623, 623/575 = 1.0835, as the note says. Engine check: forecast.py scales both pool and incidence by 1 + exus_multiple, as the note says. A labelled judgement with a case against

economics_share.source: Novo Nordisk announcement, June 2020 (https://www.novonordisk.com/content/nncorp/global/en/news-and-media/news-and-ir-materials/news-details.html?id=279; BioWorld 2020-06-11, https://www.bioworld.com/articles/435725-corvidia-therapeutics-is-sold-to-novo-for-21b): Novo acquired all outstanding shares of Corvidia Therapeutics for $725mm upfront and up to $2.1bn in total with regulatory and sales milestones. Novo's FY2025 20-F (0000353278-26-000012) lists Ziltivekimab (NN6018) in its own Phase 3 patent table
economics_share.note: Wholly owned, with no co-development or profit-share partner. The milestones to former Corvidia holders (up to about $1.375bn) are deal cash, not a revenue share, and are not in this field. Ziltivekimab was first developed by MedImmune (AstraZeneca) before Corvidia licensed it. No royalty to AstraZeneca was found in the search results or in the Novo filings the book holds. That is an absence of evidence, not a confirmed nil, so 1.0 is a ceiling. The Novo 6-K for Q2 2020 (0001628280-20-011922) appeared in search but was not opened
economics_share.check: Search excerpts (Cardiovascular Business, pharmaphorum, Novo's news item 279) confirm the purchase of Corvidia for $725mm upfront and up to $2.1bn with regulatory and sales milestones. Corvidia was spun out of AstraZeneca. The book's Novo FY2025 20-F (0000353278-26-000012, filing_sections) lists 'Ziltivekimab (NN6018) / Cardiovascular, Phase 3 initiated in 2021, 2035' in Novo's own patent/exclusivity table, and no Novo filing text in the book names a partner or a royalty. I found no AstraZeneca royalty either. As the researcher says, that is absence of evidence, and 1.0 is a ceiling. Wholly owned, so 1.0 holds

prevalence.source: CDC Heart Disease Facts (https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/data-research/facts-stats/index.html): about 805,000 people in the US have a heart attack every year. lookup.py pool 'Myocardial Infarction' returns nothing, so the book carries no pool for this disease
prevalence.note: Judgement, a convention rather than an epidemiological prevalence. The label will start treatment within 36-48 hours of an acute MI, so the addressable pool is each year's heart attacks. The living post-MI population cannot be started on the drug later under a label written from ARTEMIS. Set equal to incidence, the form forecast.py reads as a pool of the year's own events. With untreated_carryover_pct at 0 the engine zeroes the opening pool anyway, so this value does not move the forecast. Case against: a future asset for chronic post-MI prevention would need the true stock of people with a prior MI. This field would then need replacing. I did not find an AHA prevalence figure in search
prevalence.check: Pool check as asked. lookup.py pool 'Myocardial Infarction' returns nothing: no assumption row, and no epidemiology.csv row, including under 'ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction' or 'Non-ST Elevated Myocardial Infarction'. indication_groups holds only the obesity group, so nothing ties MI to another pool. lookup.py pool 'Hypercholesterolemia' returns the AZD0780 and enlicitide rows: prevalence 23,761,066 (8.9% of 266,978,268 adults with ASCVD) and incidence 1,135,700 = 605,000 first heart attacks + 0.87 x 610,000 first strokes (recomputed exact). Those 605,000 come from the same CDC Heart Disease Facts page cited here (confirmed by search: 805,000 a year, of which 605,000 first and 200,000 recurrent). So the book carries one heart-attack source, not two figures for one disease. 805,000 = 605,000 + 200,000. The ASCVD pool takes only first MIs because a recurrent-MI patient is already in its 23.8mm prevalent stock. The MI pool takes all MIs because ARTEMIS admits recurrent ones: 'any prior myocardial infarction' is one of its qualifying risk enhancers (search excerpt of the NCT06118281 criteria). Setting prevalence = incidence = 805,000 is the line-of-therapy form forecast.py reads: abs(prevalence - incidence) < 0.5. With untreated_carryover_pct stated 0.0 the engine sets the opening pool to 0 (the 'carryover == 0 and pool' branch), so this value does not move the forecast. Judgement labelled. The researcher's own case against stands: a future chronic post-MI asset needing the living stock with prior MI would have to replace this figure, not add a second

incidence.source: CDC Heart Disease Facts (https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/data-research/facts-stats/index.html): 'Every year, about 805,000 people in the United States have a heart attack. Of these, 605,000 are a first heart attack. 200,000 happen to people who have already had a heart attack.' The same page the AZD0780 and enlicitide seeds cite for 605,000 first heart attacks
incidence.note: First and recurrent heart attacks both count: ARTEMIS takes a prior MI as one of its qualifying risk criteria. About 1 in 5 are silent (same CDC page). eligible_pct removes those
incidence.check: CDC Heart Disease Facts (cdc.gov/heart-disease/data-research/facts-stats), from a search excerpt: 'Every year, about 805,000 people in the United States have a heart attack. Of these, 605,000 are a first heart attack. 200,000 happen to people who have already had a heart attack.' That is the same page the AZD0780 and enlicitide Hypercholesterolemia incidence cites for 605,000 (lookup.py pool). Counting recurrent MIs is right for this label, since prior MI qualifies a patient for ARTEMIS. This is the single MI incidence the book would carry, and it reconciles exactly to the book's 605,000

eligible_pct.source: Two filters. (1) Hospitalised: 6,603,709 US AMI hospitalisations over 2004-2014 in the National Inpatient Sample (Matetic A et al., Am J Cardiol 2020;129:10-18, doi:10.1016/j.amjcard.2020.05.025, PMID 32576369), 600,337 a year, which is 0.7458 of the CDC 805,000. (2) Type 1 MI confirmed by invasive angiography, an ARTEMIS entry criterion: coronary angiography was done in 63.4% (lowest income quartile) to 64.3% (highest) of those hospitalisations (same paper). The midpoint, 0.6385, is used. 0.7458 x 0.6385 = 0.476, about 383,000 patients a year
eligible_pct.note: Judgement on the midpoint of the angiography range. Two further ARTEMIS criteria are not applied, because no source for their share was found: symptom onset within 12 hours (STEMI) or 24 hours (NSTEMI) before admission, and at least one risk enhancer (prior MI, prior revascularisation, treated diabetes, CKD, prior ischaemic stroke, carotid disease, PAD or multivessel disease). The enhancers are broad, but both filters cut the pool, so 0.476 is an upper bound on them. Case for lower: NIS counts admissions, so transfers between hospitals are counted twice, and AMI admissions have fallen since 2004-2014. Among NSTEMI admissions in 2016-2021 only 42.7% had angiography (Borovac JA et al., Cardiovasc Revasc Med 2025;75:98-104, doi:10.1016/j.carrev.2025.03.006), partly because ICD-10 codes type 2 MI as NSTEMI. Case for higher: a label may read 'adults with acute MI' without the angiography condition
eligible_pct.check: Matetic A et al., Am J Cardiol 2020;129:10-18 (PMID 32576369, doi 10.1016/j.amjcard.2020.05.025), abstract: 6,603,709 AMI hospitalisations in NIS 2004-2014; coronary angiography 63.4% in the lowest income quartile against 64.3% in the highest. Recomputed: 6,603,709 / 11 = 600,337, and 600,337 / 805,000 = 0.74576. Midpoint 0.6385. 0.74576 x 0.6385 = 0.47617, about 383,315 patients a year. The ARTEMIS criterion checks out in search excerpts: hospitalised for acute MI, with type 1 MI shown by invasive angiography at a PCI-capable site. Borovac JA et al., Cardiovasc Revasc Med 2025;75:98-104 (PMID 40082138): 1,811,545 of 4,238,570 NSTEMI admissions (42.7%) had angiography in 2016-2021, as the case for lower says. Only the two extreme quartiles are published, so the midpoint is a labelled judgement. The unapplied symptom-onset and risk-enhancer filters are disclosed, so this reads as an upper bound

untreated_carryover_pct.source: forecast.py convention for a treatment started at an event (the line-of-therapy form): a patient not started this year does not stay eligible the next
untreated_carryover_pct.note: ARTEMIS starts the drug within 36-48 hours of admission, so a heart-attack patient not started at the index event leaves the pool. Stated outright so the engine does not carry each year's untreated patients forward
untreated_carryover_pct.check: backend/forecast.py patients_for_indication: an explicitly stated carryover of 0 with a non-zero pool sets pool = 0.0 and passes carryover 0 to derive_new_patients. Each year's eligible patients are that year's alone, and the tail converges on incidence x penetration. That fits a drug started within 36-48 h of admission (ARTEMIS design, above). Stating it explicitly is redundant with prevalence = incidence, but harmless

penetration_peak_pct.unit: share of each year's eligible patients
penetration_peak_pct.source: Incumbent: PCSK9 antibodies, the injectable add-on used for secondary prevention after MI. US starts within 1 year of an MI hospitalisation, July 2015-June 2020: 0.4% in Medicare, 0.4% in Optum CDM, 0.7% in MarketScan (Sloot R et al., Epidemiology 2024;35(4):579-588, doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001730, PMID 38629975). Weighted by the NSTEMI payer mix (Medicare 62.9%, other 37.1%; Vallabhajosyula 2021, as in discontinuation_pct): 0.511%. Updated to 2024 by the class's Medicare Part D beneficiaries (lookup.py demand): Repatha 111,259 plus Praluent Pen 52,834 = 164,093 in 2020, and 459,932 plus 92,483 = 552,415 in 2024, a 3.366x rise. 0.511% x 3.366 = 1.72%
penetration_peak_pct.note: Judgement: the multiple over the updated PCSK9 rate is 1.0. Scaling by beneficiaries treats growth in the class's Medicare stock as growth in post-MI starts. With 50%+ annual discontinuation the stock settles within two to three years, so growth there mostly reflects higher starts. Scaling from 2020, the end of the study window, is conservative. The anchor is measured over all MI admissions, while the pool here is the angiography-confirmed subset, where PCSK9 users (younger, invasively managed) concentrate. Case for higher: ziltivekimab would be started in hospital at the index event with no LDL threshold to meet. A Japanese single-centre protocol lifted PCSK9 starts after AMI from 2.8% to 15.3% (Arai R et al., J Atheroscler Thromb 2025;32(11):1434-1446, doi:10.5551/jat.65731). Case for lower: ZEUS showed no MACE benefit (HR 0.99) despite full IL-6 and hsCRP suppression, and colchicine failed after MI in CLEAR SYNERGY, so cardiologists may doubt an anti-inflammatory even after a positive ARTEMIS. Payers will also meet a biologic in an 800,000-a-year population with the same restrictions they put on PCSK9s
penetration_peak_pct.check: Sloot R et al., Epidemiology 2024;35(4):579-588 (PMID 38629975, doi 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001730), abstract: PCSK9 mAb initiation within 1 year after MI, July 2015-June 2020, 0.7% MarketScan, 0.4% Optum CDM and 0.4% Medicare (aged 66+). Weights 0.629/0.371 as in discontinuation (Vallabhajosyula, confirmed). 0.629 x 0.004 + 0.371 x 0.007 = 0.5113%. Beneficiaries, from lookup.py demand: Repatha (3 presentations) 111,259 in 2020 and 459,932 in 2024; Praluent Pen 52,834 and 92,483. That gives 164,093 and 552,415, ratio 3.3665. 0.5113% x 3.3665 = 1.7213%, so 0.0172. Form matches the engine: with no carryover, peak penetration is the share of each year's eligible patients. The multiple over the anchor is labelled a judgement, with cases both ways. Arai 2025 (PMID 40399054) confirmed at 2.8% to 15.3%. One point the note does not state: giving all non-Medicare payers MarketScan's 0.7% is the generous reading. Optum CDM (commercial plus Medicare Advantage) measured 0.4%, and 0.4% x 3.3665 = 1.35%. The value stays within the judgement's range

ramp_steepness.source: book: Leqvio's CMS uptake fit (Part B beneficiaries 6,779 in 2022, 24,690 in 2023, 48,298 in 2024), k 0.657, midpoint 5 years, as carried by the olpasiran, lepodisiran, enlicitide and AZD0780 seeds
ramp_steepness.note: Reused measured cardiovascular curve, the one the book reads for every cardiovascular prevention launch. Case against: an in-hospital start written into post-MI order sets could ramp faster than an outpatient lipid injectable once guidelines adopt it
ramp_steepness.check: lookup.py seed: k 0.657 is carried by AZD0780, enlicitide, olpasiran and lepodisiran, and data/assumptions carries it for milvexian and abelacimab too, the book's cardiovascular launch curve. The Part B beneficiaries quoted are right (lookup.py demand Leqvio: 6,779 / 24,690 / 48,298 for 2022-2024). One source detail: olpasiran's k row attributes the fit to Leqvio's Part D series (721 to 2,681), and the Part B series appears in its penetration and midpoint rows. The value is the book's measured cardiovascular k either way

ramp_midpoint_year.source: as ramp_steepness (Leqvio fit carried by the olpasiran, lepodisiran and enlicitide seeds)
ramp_midpoint_year.note: Reused measured curve. forecast_start_year here is the first full year on market (2029, after an approval expected late 2028). The Leqvio series the curve was fitted to also starts in its first full year: FDA approval 2021-12-22 (NDA214012, book approvals), first CMS year 2022. So counting the 5-year midpoint from the first full year keeps the curve on its own basis and needs no shift. AZD0780 shifts to 6 only because its forecast start (2027) precedes its launch. The enlicitide seed is not the precedent: its forecast_start_year is its launch year, 2026. Case against: an in-hospital start written into post-MI order sets could ramp faster than an outpatient lipid injectable once guidelines adopt it
ramp_midpoint_year.check: Value 5.0 confirmed: olpasiran, lepodisiran and enlicitide carry midpoint 5 with k 0.657 (lookup.py seed). Olpasiran's seed says no midpoint below 5 reproduces Leqvio's 2023-2024 step at that k. Note corrected only. It said the first full year is the forecast start 'as in the enlicitide seed', but that seed's forecast_start_year is 2026, 'the launch year: FDA approval in July 2026' (lookup.py seed Enlicitide). The note now rests the no-shift on Leqvio's own basis: FDA approval 2021-12-22 (NDA214012, book approvals table), first CMS year 2022, its first full year. forecast.py indexes the curve from forecast_start_year (year index 0), so the two bases match
